AGENCY:
Enforcement and Compliance, International Trade Administration, Department of Commerce.
SUMMARY:
As a result of the determinations by the U.S. Department of Commerce (Commerce) and the U.S. International Trade Commission (ITC) that revocation of the antidumping duty (AD) and countervailing duty (CVD) orders on standard steel welded wire mesh from Mexico would likely lead to the continuation or recurrence of dumping and countervailable subsidies, and material injury to an industry in the United States, Commerce is publishing a notice of continuation of these AD and CVD orders.
DATES:
Applicable September 23, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Kayden Jenson, AD/CVD Operations, Office II, Enforcement and Compliance, International Trade Administration, U.S. Department of Commerce, 1401 Constitution Avenue NW, Washington, DC 20230; telephone: (202) 482-0967.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background
On April 12 and August 9, 2021, Commerce published in the
Federal Register
the AD and CVD orders on standard steel welded wire mesh from Mexico.[1]
On March 2, 2026, the ITC instituted,[2]
and Commerce initiated,[3]
the first sunset review of the
Orders,
pursuant to section 751(c) of the Tariff Act of 1930, as amended (the Act). As a result of its reviews, Commerce determined that revocation of the
Orders
would likely lead to the continuation or recurrence of dumping and/or countervailable subsidies, and therefore, notified the ITC of the magnitude of the margins of dumping and subsidy rates likely to prevail should the
Orders
be revoked.[4]
On September 21, 2026, the ITC published its determination, pursuant to sections 751(c) and 752(a) of the Act, that revocation of the
Orders
would likely lead to continuation or recurrence of material injury to an industry in the United States within a reasonably foreseeable time.[5]
Scope of the Orders
The merchandise covered by the scope of the orders is standard steel welded wire mesh from Mexico. For a full description of the scope of the
Orders, see
the appendix to this notice.
Continuation of the Orders
As a result of the determinations by Commerce and the ITC that revocation of the
Orders
would likely lead to continuation or recurrence of dumping, countervailable subsidies, and material injury to an industry in the United States, pursuant to section 751(d)(2) of the Act, Commerce hereby orders the continuation of the
Orders.
U.S. Customs and Border Protection will continue to collect AD and CVD cash deposits at the rates in effect at the time of entry for all imports of subject merchandise.
The effective date of the continuation of the
Orders
will be September 23, 2026.[6]
Pursuant to section 751(c)(2) of the Act and 19 CFR 351.218(c)(2), Commerce intends to initiate the next five-year reviews of the
Orders
not later than 30 days prior to fifth anniversary of the date of the last determination by the ITC.
Administrative Protective Order (APO)
This notice also serves as a final reminder to parties subject to an APO of their responsibility concerning the return or destruction of proprietary information disclosed under APO in accordance with 19 CFR 351.305(a)(3), which continues to govern business proprietary information in this segment of the proceeding. Timely written notification of the return or destruction of APO materials, or conversion to judicial protective order, is hereby requested. Failure to comply with the regulations and terms of an APO is a violation which is subject to sanction.
Notification to Interested Parties
These five-year (sunset) reviews and this notice are in accordance with sections 751(c) and 751(d)(2) of the Act, and published in accordance with section 777(i) of the Act and 19 CFR 351.218(f)(4).
Dated: October 19, 2026.
Scot Fullerton,
Acting Deputy Assistant Secretary for Antidumping and Countervailing Duty Operations.
Appendix
Scope of the Orders
The merchandise covered by this order is uncoated standard welded steel reinforcement wire mesh (wire mesh) produced from smooth or deformed wire. Subject wire mesh is produced in square and rectangular grids of uniformly spaced steel wires that are welded at all intersections.
( printed page 67275)
Sizes are specified by combining the spacing of the wires in inches or millimeters and the wire cross-sectional area in hundredths of square inch or millimeters squared. Subject wire mesh may be packaged and sold in rolls or in sheets.
Subject wire mesh is currently produced to ASTM specification A1064/A1064M, which covers carbon-steel wire and welded wire reinforcement, smooth and deformed, for concrete in the following seven styles:
1. 6X6 W1.4/W1.4 or D1.4/D1.4
2. 6X6 W2.1/W2.1 or D2.1/D2.1
3. 6X6 W2.9/W2.9 or D2.9/D2.9
4. 6X6 W4/W4 or D4/D4
5. 6X12 W4/W4 or D4/D4
6. 4X4 W2.9/W2.9 or D2.9/D2.9
7. 4X4 W4/W4 or D4/D4
The first number in the style denotes the nominal spacing between the longitudinal wires and the second number denotes the nominal spacing between the transverse wires. In the first style listed above, for example, “6X6” denotes a grid size of six inches by six inches. “W” denotes the use of smooth wire, and “D” denotes the use of deformed wire in making the mesh. The number following the W or D denotes the nominal cross-sectional area of the transverse and longitudinal wires in hundredths of a square inch (
i.e.,
W1.4 or D1.4 is .014 square inches).
Smooth wire is wire that has a uniform cross-sectional diameter throughout the length of the wire.
Deformed wire is wire with indentations or raised transverse ribs, which results in wire that does not have a uniform cross-sectional diameter throughout the length of the wire.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background
On May 4, 2021, Commerce published in the
Federal Register
the
Orders
on small vertical engines from China.[1]
On April 1, 2026, Commerce initiated the first sunset review of the
Orders,
pursuant to section 751(c) of the Tariff Act of 1930, as amended (the Act).[2]
As a result of its reviews, Commerce determined that revocation of the
Orders
would likely lead to the continuation or recurrence of dumping and countervailable subsidies, and therefore, notified the ITC of the magnitude of the margin of dumping and subsidy rates likely to prevail should the
Orders
be revoked.[3]
On October 20, 2026, the ITC published its determination, pursuant to sections 751(c) and 752(a) of the Act, that revocation of the
Orders
would likely lead to continuation or recurrence of material injury to an industry in the United States within a reasonably foreseeable time.[4]
Scope of the Orders
The scope of the
Orders
consists of spark-ignited, non-road, vertical shaft engines, whether finished or unfinished, whether assembled or unassembled, whether mounted or unmounted, primarily for walk-behind lawn mowers. Engines meeting this physical description may also be for other non-hand-held outdoor power equipment, including but not limited to, pressure washers. The subject engines are spark ignition, single-cylinder, air cooled, internal combustion engines with vertical power take off shafts with a minimum displacement of 99 cubic centimeters (cc) and a maximum displacement of up to, but not including, 225cc. Typically, engines with displacements of this size generate gross power of between 1.95 kilowatts (kw) to 4.75 kw.
Engines covered by this scope normally must comply with and be certified under Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) air pollution controls title 40, chapter I, subchapter U, part 1054 of the Code of Federal Regulations standards for small non-road spark-ignition engines and equipment. Engines that otherwise meet the physical description of the scope but are not certified under 40 CFR part 1054 and are not certified under other parts of subchapter U of the EPA air pollution controls are not excluded from the scope of these proceedings. Engines that may be certified under both 40 CFR part 1054 as well as other parts of subchapter U remain subject to the scope of these proceedings.
Certain small vertical shaft engines, whether or not mounted on non-hand-held outdoor power equipment, including but not limited to walk-behind lawn mowers and pressure washers, are included in the scope. However, if a subject engine is imported mounted on such equipment, only the engine is covered by the scope. Subject merchandise includes certain small vertical shaft engines produced in the subject country whether mounted on outdoor power equipment in the subject country or in a third country. Subject engines are covered whether or not they are accompanied by other parts.
For purposes of these
Orders,
an unfinished engine covers at a minimum a sub-assembly comprised of, but not limited to, the following components: Crankcase, crankshaft, camshaft, piston(s), and connecting rod(s). Importation of these components together, whether assembled or unassembled, and whether or not accompanied by additional components such as a sump, carburetor spacer, cylinder head(s), valve train, or valve cover(s), constitutes an unfinished engine for purposes of these
Orders.
The inclusion of other products such as spark plugs fitted into the cylinder head or electrical devices (
e.g.,
ignition coils) for synchronizing with the engine to supply tension current does not remove the product from the scope. The inclusion of any other components not identified as comprising the unfinished engine subassembly in a third country does not remove the engine from the scope.
Specifically excluded from the scope of these

Orders

high_priority_articles.title: Pakistan textile exporters warn EU-India trade deal could erode market advantage - Arab News PK
high_priority_articles.summary: Pakistan textile exporters warn EU-India trade deal could erode market advantage  Arab News PK
high_priority_articles.full_text:
- SITE industry chief warns rising production costs could undermine Pakistan’s textile export growth
- India’s trade agreement with EU could take effect in early 2027, narrowing Pakistan’s tariff advantage
KARACHI: Pakistan’s textile exporters risk losing their competitive advantage in European markets as improved trade access for rival countries and rising production costs threaten the sector, a leading industry representative warned on Saturday, urging the government to lower manufacturing costs and pursue new export markets.
The warning comes as the European Union prepares to implement a free trade agreement with India that could reduce Pakistan’s relative tariff advantage under the bloc’s Generalized Scheme of Preferences Plus (GSP+). India and the EU concluded negotiations in January, and India’s trade minister said on Thursday the agreement could become operational in early 2027.
SITE Association of Industry (SAI) President Abdul Hadi said Pakistan’s textile and apparel exports had grown in the first quarter of the current fiscal year, but high operating costs and increasing regional competition threatened to undermine further gains.
“Exports rose 5.26pc year-on-year to $5.026 billion in the first quarter of FY27, but rising production costs and competition from regional exporters could undermine this growth,” Hadi said in a statement, citing industry figures.
Pakistan’s textile and clothing industry is the country’s largest export sector and a major source of employment and foreign exchange earnings. The European Union is among its most important markets, with preferential access under GSP+ allowing a substantial share of Pakistani goods to enter the bloc duty-free.
Hadi said Pakistan could not rely indefinitely on existing trade preferences and needed to improve productivity, product quality and industrial efficiency to remain competitive.
He urged the government to strengthen trade diplomacy, secure access to additional export markets and reduce the cost of doing business.
According to figures cited by the association, Pakistan’s textile and apparel exports reached approximately $18 billion in the fiscal year ending June 2026. The sector accounts for around 60 percent of the country’s export earnings, the association said.
Hadi said Pakistan remained heavily dependent on relatively low-value-added products, including yarn, fabric and basic home textiles, limiting its ability to earn higher returns in international markets.
He called for greater investment in technical textiles, branded apparel and other higher-margin products, alongside modern technology and improvements in manufacturing productivity.
The SITE chief also expressed concern over declining domestic cotton production, which he said had increased the textile industry’s dependence on imported raw materials.
He also urged the government to improve domestic cotton production and strengthen coordination between the agricultural and industrial sectors to ensure a reliable supply of quality raw materials at competitive prices.

high_priority_articles.summary: Bipartisan US Lawmakers Push Back On Trump's Russia Policy, Vow Support For Ukraine  Radio Free Europe/Radio LibertyTrump’s Overtures to Putin Put Republican Candidates in Hot Seat  WSJGOP’s Don Bacon rips Trump over ‘disgraceful’ behavior on Ukraine, Russia  The HillRubio says Trump to take up to 60 days to weigh Russia sanctions  ReutersRepublicans revolt over Trump’s sanctions waiver for Russia  The Times
high_priority_articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON -- A bipartisan group of US lawmakers is stepping up efforts to defend Ukraine, challenging President Donald Trump’s decision to ease restrictions on Russian energy imports and demanding guarantees that Kyiv will retain access to critical American military and intelligence support.
In a series of legislative initiatives, congressional inquiries, and appeals to the administration, Republicans and Democrats have warned that decisions benefiting Moscow or disrupting Ukraine’s battlefield capabilities could undermine US national security, weaken congressional authority, and prolong Russia’s war.
The pushback comes after the administration authorized transactions involving Russian diesel fuel, amid reports that Ukraine’s access to SpaceX’s Starlink and military-grade Starshield satellite communications systems had been restricted.
Ukrainian officials say the disruptions have affected military operations, although they reported on October 24 that satellite connection speeds had been restored. Questions remain about who imposed the restrictions.
A Ukrainian official familiar with the matter told RFE/RL that SpaceX had not responded to Kyiv about the previous restrictions. The official added that although Kyiv had been in touch with the US government, "no one has explained what happened or what will happen next."
The developments have exposed growing divisions over the administration’s Russia policy, with some Republicans joining Democrats in demanding accountability and stronger safeguards for Ukraine.
Bill Targets Russian Oil Waiver
Representative Brian Fitzpatrick, a Pennsylvania Republican and co-chair of the Congressional Ukraine Caucus, has introduced the Ronald Reagan Peace Through Strength Act of 2026, alongside Republican Representative Don Bacon of Nebraska and Democratic Representative Marie Gluesenkamp Perez of Washington.
The bill would nullify a Treasury Department waiver issued on October 9 that authorized transactions involving Russian diesel fuel, including imports into the United States. The temporary authorization is due to expire on April 7, 2027.
Trump has defended the agreement with Russia as a way to increase global diesel supplies and bring down fuel prices. Announcing the deal on October 9 following talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin, he said Russia had agreed to immediately supply more than 300,000 metric tons of diesel to US and global markets, with further shipments to follow. Diesel prices have risen sharply amid disruptions to global energy supplies linked to the war in Iran.
The proposed bill would also prohibit future waivers allowing Russian energy imports and require intelligence agencies to provide support for Ukraine’s defense, notifying congressional intelligence committees within 24 hours of any interruption.
The legislation seeks to reinforce a 2022 federal law prohibiting Russian oil imports, which the sponsors say the administration has undermined through its latest decision.
“Congress must be a check to the president’s egregious appeasement to Putin,” Bacon told RFE/RL.
In a statement announcing the bill, Fitzpatrick argued that Washington could not credibly demand accountability from Russian President Vladimir Putin while allowing American markets to support the energy revenues sustaining his war.
“We must not import a single drop of Russian oil,” Fitzpatrick said, adding that Congress had approved the prohibition with overwhelming bipartisan support in 2022.
He invoked the late President Reagan’s foreign policy doctrine, arguing that strength was necessary to secure peace and that aggression must carry a cost greater than its rewards.
Bacon accused Trump of reversing his own criticism of European countries for purchasing Russian energy.
“For years, President Trump criticized Europe for buying Russian energy and propping up Putin’s war economy,” Bacon said. “Now, Trump wants to make it easier for Putin to sell diesel fuel. He is wrong.”
Gluesenkamp Perez also condemned the waiver, saying it ran roughshod over American national interests and the bipartisan will of Congress. She argued that if Trump wanted to reduce gasoline prices, he should pursue policies that end the war in Iran rather than direct American money toward Russia.
The bill has been referred to three House committees for consideration. Its introduction marks one of the first legislative responses to the administration’s recent Russia-related decisions.
Lawmakers Press Pentagon Over Ukraine Satellite Access
Concern over Ukraine’s military capabilities has also brought together lawmakers from both parties in the House and Senate.
Eight lawmakers -- Representatives Marcy Kaptur (Dem.-Ohio), Brian Fitzpatrick (Rep.-Pennsylvania), Mike Quigley (Dem.-Illinois), Jim Costa (Dem.-California), and Jimmy Panetta (Dem.-California), along with Senators Mark Kelly (Dem.-Arizona), Thom Tillis (Rep.-North Carolina), and Elissa Slotkin (Dem.-Michigan) -- have urged Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to expand the Pentagon’s Starshield contract and ensure uninterrupted access to Starlink and Starshield services.
The lawmakers called for the restoration of unrestricted service speeds, sufficient geographic coverage for Ukraine’s lawful military operations, including over Russian territory, and a seamless transition from commercial Starlink to government-contracted Starshield.
“Any degradation in service, including reduced connection speeds, restricted geographic coverage, or interruptions in access, undermines Ukraine’s military effectiveness and provides Russian forces with an operational advantage that will extend the conflict and put more civilians in harm’s way,” they wrote.
They also urged the Defense Department to consider using its authority under the Defense Production Act to ensure reliable access to the satellite communications on which Ukrainian forces depend for command and control, intelligence sharing, battlefield communications and drone operations.
“Decisions regarding service availability, coverage, and performance should not be left solely to the discretion of a private provider when they have direct consequences for Ukraine’s ability to defend itself,” the lawmakers said.
The appeal followed Ukrainian reports that restrictions introduced on October 13 disrupted communications for drones and other military platforms moving faster than 100 miles per hour (160 km/h), affecting Ukraine’s ability to guide defensive drones and conduct operations against Russian positions.
Musk Faces Questions Over Ukraine Satellite Restrictions
The satellite dispute has prompted additional congressional investigations into who ordered the restrictions and whether the US government has sufficient oversight of the communications systems it relies on.
New York Representative Gregory Meeks, the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, and Democratic Senator Peter Welch of Vermont have led a group of six Democratic lawmakers demanding answers from SpaceX chief executive Elon Musk.
Their letter questions Musk’s public assertion that restrictions were determined by the US military and ultimately the president, citing reports that Musk himself proposed limiting Ukrainian communications.
The lawmakers have asked whether Musk or SpaceX officials discussed restricting access with Trump, Putin, or their representatives; who ordered any limitations; what conditions Ukraine must meet to regain full access; and who will control future operational decisions.
They also raised concerns about corporate governance and the implications of a private company exercising decisive influence over a foreign military’s communications.
Connecticut Senator Richard Blumenthal, the top Democrat on the Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, has separately opened a congressional inquiry, demanding written answers from Musk by November 5 and a briefing from SpaceX officials by November 12.
Blumenthal is seeking details about who authorized the restrictions, whether Ukraine received advance notice, and whether SpaceX can degrade Starshield service for US or allied forces without Pentagon authorization. He has also requested information on the value of SpaceX’s government contracts since 2020.
Separately, Democratic Representatives Sam Liccardo and Ro Khanna of California, along with Panetta, have called on White House chief of staff Susie Wiles to initiate a government-wide investigation and provide a briefing within two weeks.
“Either a private contractor independently made life-and-death national security decisions, or President Trump directed the restriction of critical military communications supporting a US ally,” they wrote.
The demands for answers come amid conflicting accounts of who authorized the restrictions.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio has denied that Trump or other administration officials ordered them or knew about them in advance. Musk, meanwhile, has said Starshield systems are controlled by the US government and that decisions on restrictions ultimately rest with the military and the president.
Trump has said service was restored following contact with Musk, but Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has disputed that account, saying restrictions remain in place.
The uncertainty has also drawn criticism from Republican Senator Thom Tillis, who wrote on X: “Whoever is handing Putin the gift of a more vulnerable Ukraine should at least have the guts to put their name on it.”

high_priority_articles.summary: China Imposes Export Control on Tunnel Boring Machines in What Indian Expert Calls ‘Covert Trade War’  Vision Times
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Citing national security interests, China’s Ministry of Commerce said in an announcement on Oct. 19 that it was imposing export controls on tunnel-boring machines and related items destined for “sensitive countries” and regions with which China has disputes. An Indian expert described the move as a surprise and a “secret trade war” and called for a comprehensive response from New Delhi.
“China will impose export controls on full-face tunnel-boring machines, including earth-pressure-balance, slurry-balance and other shield machines, as well as open, single-shield and double-shield rock tunnel-boring machines,” the ministry said in a release on Monday, Oct. 20.
India and China share a long, disputed border along the Himalayan mountain range, which separates the Tibetan Plateau from the Indian subcontinent. Following the deadly 2020 Galwan Valley clash, in which soldiers from both countries were killed, India and China accelerated infrastructure development along the border, including the construction of roads, railways, tunnels and bridges.
This is where China’s export controls on heavy equipment and machinery become geopolitically sensitive. According to the official announcement, the controls cover machines designed for use at altitudes above 3,000 meters.
The controls also cover specified engines, motors, compressors, chassis, folding arms and related hydraulic and pumping technologies. Exports of these items to “sensitive countries and regions with which China has disputes” require an export license from the Ministry of Commerce, according to the announcement.

Banuchandar Nagarajan, an Indian public policy adviser, told Vision Times that “the latest export ban or export restrictions on tunnel-boring machines are part of China’s unannounced, covert trade war with India,”
“They inflict a double whammy: on one side, they restrict access to critical minerals and components, making it difficult to manufacture machines and tools in India. On the other side, they also impose restrictions on finished products.”
In an August 2025 parliamentary response in the Lok Sabha, India’s Ministry of Commerce and Industry confirmed that China’s export controls on rare-earth magnets had caused supply-chain bottlenecks affecting Indian industries, including electric vehicle (EV) manufacturers, the Press Trust of India (PTI) reported.
Nagarajan said such restrictions had occurred many times before, including restrictions involving carbide tools—industrial cutting, drilling and machining tools made primarily from cemented carbide, a high-performance composite material.
“There is a restriction on tungsten carbide exports to India, and at the same time, they keep dumping low-cost tools into India, thereby hurting our local manufacturers.
“Unfortunately, even the government has turned a blind eye to this when it comes to procurement, where government bids are based on L1 [lowest bidder] and not the total cost of ownership,” he said.
Nagarajan called for a “comprehensive” response from Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s administration and outlined four measures that should form its basis.
“First, the critical minerals partnership, on which the government is already taking steps. Second, making sure that we develop these advanced manufacturing capabilities so that we produce these machines as part of Atmanirbhar Bharat.”
Atmanirbhar Bharat, meaning “self-reliant India,” is an initiative launched by Modi in May 2020 to strengthen domestic manufacturing, reduce excessive dependence on imports and make the country more resilient to global supply-chain disruptions.
“Third, we make sure that we have anti-dumping import controls on Chinese goods. Fourth, government entities and PSUs don’t procure Chinese goods just because they are cheap based on L1 bids,” Nagarajan said.
Meanwhile, Indian government officials have said they would consult industry stakeholders on an appropriate response to China’s export controls on heavy equipment and machinery, including tunnel-boring machines and related items. They have also ruled out any significant impact on highway construction in India, according to The Economic Times, a major Indian daily.

high_priority_articles.title: Russia-Azerbaijan Economic Relations Shift Towards Investment, Trade Recovery and Regional Logistics - Modern Ghana
high_priority_articles.summary: Russia-Azerbaijan Economic Relations Shift Towards Investment, Trade Recovery and Regional Logistics  Modern Ghana
high_priority_articles.full_text:
The deterioration in trade follows several years of political and diplomatic friction, including the December 2024 Azerbaijani aircraft disaster, disagreements surrounding Karabakh and tensions following the detention of Azerbaijani diaspora members in Russia in 2025. Concerns about secondary sanctions and Azerbaijan’s efforts to diversify its strategic partnerships have added further complications. Nevertheless, bilateral trade totalled US$4.92 billion in 2025, an increase of 2.5% over 2024, demonstrating the underlying importance of the relationship. Russia was Azerbaijan’s third-largest foreign-trade partner, accounting for 9.96% of its total trade. The current decline therefore represents a significant commercial challenge, but not necessarily a permanent retreat from economic cooperation.
Agriculture remains one of the strongest foundations for maintaining trade flows. Russia purchased more than US$1.174 billion in Azerbaijani non-oil products in 2025, including agricultural exports exceeding US$837 million. Fruit and vegetable shipments alone reached US$696 million, supported by increasing demand for Azerbaijani produce. During early 2026, Russian imports of onions from Azerbaijan rose sharply, while strawberry, potato and pear shipments also recorded increases. Meanwhile, Russian agricultural supplies to Azerbaijan exceeded US$832 million, illustrating the reciprocal nature of agricultural trade. These established commercial relationships offer opportunities to stabilise bilateral turnover while political and administrative obstacles are addressed.
Investment developments present a more positive picture. Russian direct investment in Azerbaijan reached US$237.119 million in the first half of 2026, an increase of 82.8% from US$129.727 million during the corresponding period of 2025. Russia accounted for 6.5% of foreign direct investment entering Azerbaijan during the period. By contrast, Azerbaijani investment in Russia fell 20.6% to US$22.488 million. Accumulated Russian investment in Azerbaijan has been reported at approximately US$10.7 billion, including US$2.9 billion in the non-oil economy, while more than 1,400 Russian-capitalised companies were registered as active in Azerbaijan in April 2026. These businesses provide a foundation for expanding manufacturing, distribution, services and other commercial activities, although rising investment alone cannot compensate for declining merchandise trade.
The September and October diplomatic engagements reflect efforts to translate this economic foundation into practical results. On September 26, Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak met Azerbaijani Deputy Prime Minister Shahin Mustafayev in Baku to discuss industry, energy, transport and logistics. On October 5, Mustafayev and Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexei Overchuk chaired intergovernmental discussions in Moscow, focusing on trade, investment, border-crossing capacity, freight transportation and the implementation of existing agreements. The October 9 meeting between Russian President Vladimir Putin, Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian in Turkmenistan further highlighted the importance of regional economic coordination. Although these engagements did not establish a new quantified trilateral infrastructure package, they reinforced the political framework for cooperation.
The INSTC is central to this emerging agenda. Azerbaijan provides a strategic overland link between Russia and Iran, connecting northern markets with the Persian Gulf, India and wider South Asian destinations. Improving customs procedures, freight handling, railway operations and border-crossing efficiency could reduce transport costs and make the corridor more competitive. September 2026 freight traffic on the Russian-Azerbaijani border averaged approximately 840 cargo vehicles daily, while the reconstructed Yarag-Kazmalyar crossing reportedly increased potential border capacity from around 400 to 1,900 freight vehicles per day. However, infrastructure capacity must be matched by efficient administration, predictable transit times and commercially viable transport services.
Completing the approximately 160-kilometre Rasht-Astara railway section in Iran remains a major challenge for the corridor’s western route. The project has faced delays associated with land acquisition and administrative procedures, with completion targeted for 2030. Meanwhile, declining Caspian Sea water levels pose additional risks to maritime transport, port operations and regional logistics investment. Competing connectivity initiatives, including the proposed Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity (TRIPP), also illustrate how geopolitical interests and infrastructure ownership are shaping the South Caucasus transport landscape.
As highlighted by Russia’s Pivot to Asia, the central question is whether renewed diplomatic engagement can generate measurable commercial improvements. Priorities include reversing the decline in Russian exports to Azerbaijan, sustaining Azerbaijani non-oil exports, converting investment into productive capacity and resolving transport bottlenecks. The relationship increasingly depends on three interconnected factors: established trade networks, expanding investment and Azerbaijan’s geographical position between Russia and Iran. The autumn meetings have established a framework for cooperation, but long-term success will depend on implementing existing commitments, completing critical infrastructure and restoring sustainable growth in bilateral trade.

(Kitco News) – Gold prices suffered another sharp weekly decline as rising oil prices, persistent inflation fears, and expectations for further Federal Reserve tightening overwhelmed safe-haven demand, while Thursday's technology-led equity selloff triggered another wave of liquidations that pushed the precious metal back below $4,000 per ounce.
Spot gold kicked off the week trading at $4,164.69 per ounce on Sunday evening, and the yellow metal managed to eke out some early gains as traders continued to assess renewed U.S.-Iran tensions and the inflationary impact of disruptions around the Strait of Hormuz. But the rally quickly stalled, with gold setting its weekly high of $4,190.17 per ounce early Monday morning before sellers took control as rising energy prices and elevated Treasury yields reinforced expectations that the Fed would maintain their restrictive monetary policy.
The selling accelerated through Monday and Tuesday trading, with gold breaking below $4,150 as markets continued to digest the previous week's hotter-than-expected CPI and PPI reports. The yellow metal attempted to stabilize on Wednesday as Treasury yields eased, but the recovery proved short-lived as traders remained focused on the risk of another Fed rate hike before year-end.
Gold prices plunged Thursday as a sharp technology-led equity selloff triggered broader market liquidations, even as Treasury yields and the dollar weakened. Renewed concerns about the AI sector and speculation about possible intervention in the Japanese yen added to the uncertainty, while renewed Middle East tensions pushed oil prices higher. The selling carried over into Friday, with gold set its weekly low of $3,975.10 per ounce – its lowest level since early June – around an hour after the North American open, and prices oscillated on both sides of $4,000-per-ounce heading into the weekly close.
The latest Kitco News Weekly Gold Survey showed Wall Street pessimism on the rise after gold’s steep slide, while Main Street saw more silver lining despite the yellow metal’s recent underperformance.
“Gold, basis spot, was sold to a new three-month low before the weekend, slightly below $3990,” said Marc Chandler, managing director at Bannockburn Global Forex. “It recovered but the technical tone still looks weak. The momentum indicators are not rising and the five- and 20-day moving averages are falling. Initial resistance is seen in the 4065-4075 area.”
“Half of the G10 central banks meet next week and only the RBNZ is likely to hike,” Chandler added. “Still, the others, including the Fed, will keep the door open to hikes before the end of the year.”
“Unchanged,” said Adrian Day, president of Adrian Day Asset Management. “More back and forth, but still think $4,000 will hold, or maybe just a little below.”
“Up,” said James Stanley, senior market strategist at Forex.com. “The $4k test has held so far, and while it may take a bit for the tide to turn, I think the case is still strong for $4k support – unless something breaks in the US economy which could lead to a risk aversion run. But even in that backdrop, I’m biased towards longer-term accumulation.”
“Up,” said Rich Checkan, president and COO of Asset Strategies International. “The sell-off in the stock market this week triggered margin calls. As always, investors seeking liquidity to meet those margin calls turned to THE most liquid asset on earth… gold. The selling pressure took gold back below $4,000 per ounce.”
“I do not expect gold to remain below $4,000 very long,” Checkan said. “Barring any surprises from next Wednesday’s interest rate announcement from the Federal Open Market Committee, I would expect gold to bounce off these lows as bargain hunters snatch up as much cheap gold as they are able.”
Kevin Grady, president of Phoenix Futures and Options, said gold continues to trade inversely to interest rates, but there’s also broader concerns impacting the yellow metal.
“We're all thinking about rates, and I know we're following daily yields and things like that,” he said. “But it's also the long-term picture that people are looking at and seeing that there is a crack in the bond market, and even historically, that rates are higher.”
It's hard to see, because you're not really getting a lot of color,” Grady said. “A lot of commercials have decreased their trading. You're not seeing the volumes that we've had in the past. I think it's one of those things where gold has been trying to see the next leg up, and we just haven't had it.”
Grady said that a number of longs came into the market as gold posted its recent gains, and they were waiting for a good exit, but it didn’t come, and now they have no choice but to exit at lower prices and into thin liquidity.
“When you look at daily volumes at 129,000 contracts, that's what we used to do in open outcry! Once the markets went electronic, we were doing over 400,000 easily,” he said. “I think what's happening now is that it's very thin, and when you see people start to get out, it's just exacerbated the moves.”
Grady said that between the Iran war’s renewed threats of escalation, Russia-Ukraine getting worse, the risk of a hawkish Fed next week, and the looming midterm elections, people are wary of putting their money into the markets – any markets.
“That move [on Thursday], I think scared a lot of people away from saying, ‘Hey, let me go in right before a big meeting or a big decision where I don't know where it's going to be, and let me take a position.’ Because getting out of that position can be deadly.”
“I think that move yesterday is going to put a lot of people on the sidelines.”
Turning to Wednesday’s Fed meeting, Grady said that even if markets are pricing in a hold, under current conditions, they really can’t be sure
“What is the Fed going to do? The market's saying, no, he's not going to raise rates, but maybe he tries to shock people,” he said. “I don't think he should, but you just don't know. There's just too much uncertainty. A lot of people, especially professional traders, are saying, ‘This isn't trading right now, it's guessing.’”
“I was speaking with a friend of mine yesterday who's a big trader on the floor with me, in gold, and we were talking about [this],” he said “It isn't just that you’re a trader and you're putting on positions. As a trader, you're a risk manager. And if you're not a good risk manager, you're not going to be a successful trader. I think right now, when you look at the upside or downside to putting on a trade, what are the odds of this trade working? Markets have gotten so thin… I just think the upside is not worth it.”
Grady said that if gold does see a break below $4,000, we’ll soon be approaching levels where prices held during earlier selloffs.
“But I will tell you, underneath those levels is going to be stops, and everyone knows that,” he said. “Being long in front of those… it's always nice to buy in front of the support level, but when it breaks that support level, it could be dangerous. So I think people have to really watch out.”
This week, 17 analysts participated in the Kitco News Gold Survey, with the largest portion of Wall Street sentiment sliding into the bearish camp after gold’s precipitous drop below $4,000. Four experts, or 24%, expect to see gold prices gain ground during the week ahead, while seven, representing 41%, see the yellow metal declining further. The remaining six analysts, 35% of the total, said they couldn’t predict gold’s direction, or expected sideways trading next week.
Meanwhile, 161 votes were cast in Kitco’s online poll, with Main Street investors considerably more bullish than their professional counterparts despite gold’s late-week slide. 67 retail traders, or 42%, looked for gold prices to rise next week, while 41 others, or 26%, predicted the yellow metal would lose more ground. Then on Wednesday morning, the Bank of Canada will issue its monetary policy decision, followed by the Federal Reserve’s monetary policy decision in the afternoon.
Thursday morning will see the ECB’s monetary policy decision, along with Advance US Q3 GDP and PCE, and weekly jobless claims, with the Bank of Japan’s monetary policy decision coming overnight to cap the week’s key data.
Sean Lusk, co-director of commercial hedging at Walsh Trading, said the Iran conflict – and its impact on oil prices, inflation expectations, and Fed rate projections – continues to cap gold’s potential gains.

By Sergio Goncalves and Miguel Pereira
LISBON, Oct 23 (Reuters) – Thailand welcomes US engagement with Myanmar and expects discussions at the Association of Southeast Asian Nations’ November summit in Manila on how to proceed with the member barred since the 2021 coup, Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow told Reuters on Friday.
The United States and Myanmar’s military-backed government held talks in Tokyo two weeks ago, their second meeting in a month as Washington steps up re-engagement with the generals it shunned after the coup.
“We don’t want to see Myanmar isolated, we don’t want Myanmar to be an arena for geopolitical rivalry … so the US engagement is something that we welcome,” he said.
Engagement “does not mean legitimizing the regime,” but aims to encourage peaceful conflict resolution and reconciliation with the opposition, Sihasak, who is also deputy prime minister, added.
He said there was “some shift in ASEAN’s position,” citing Myanmar President Min Aung Hlaing’s recent visits to Laos, Cambodia, Vietnam, Thailand and Malaysia, but said it was unclear whether the Manila summit would address restoring Myanmar’s full representation.
“It’s good that we’re going to have a very substantive, very extensive, and very in-depth discussion on how to proceed on Myanmar,” he said.
He also said Thailand and Cambodia could resolve their longstanding land and maritime boundary disputes within 12 to 18 months despite limited progress.
“It is possible, everything is possible,” he said, cautioning that confidence-building and addressing security concerns along the land border, where clashes have occurred, must come first.
Cambodia launched a conciliation process under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea in June to resolve the maritime boundary dispute, after Thailand terminated a 2001 joint development framework in May following deadly border clashes. The first meeting was held about a month ago.
“Right now, we haven’t achieved, to be very frank, much progress,” he said.
The maritime dispute centers on overlapping claims to about 26,000 sq km in the Gulf of Thailand, believed to hold oil and gas reserves worth around $300 billion. Thailand wants the boundary defined before discussing resource-sharing, he said.
Thailand-EU free-trade talks are in their final stage and could conclude by year-end if there is mutual political will, he added.

New Delhi: Union Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal strongly criticised Europe's climate policies on Friday, arguing that developed nations bear greater historical responsibility for global carbon emissions and climate change.
Speaking at the Berlin Global Dialogue 2026, Goyal warned that Europe's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) and high steel import duties could increase living costs and weaken industrial competitiveness.
Piyush Goyal Questions Europe's Climate Responsibility
During a panel discussion, Goyal questioned developed countries' historical contribution to the climate crisis. He argued that India supports approximately 17 per cent of the global population but contributes less than 3 per cent of carbon emissions.
In contrast, he said Europe's contribution to global emissions has been disproportionately high compared with its population. Goyal maintained that developed economies relied heavily on inexpensive fossil fuels during their industrial expansion.
CBAM And Steel Tariffs Could Raise Costs
The minister criticised Europe's carbon border tax and steel import restrictions, warning that such measures could affect businesses and consumers. He argued that imposing additional costs on imported products could make European industries less competitive while increasing household expenses. Goyal also highlighted India's growing renewable energy programme and commitment to sustainable development.
India Raises Climate Finance Concerns
Referring to the 2015 Paris Agreement, Goyal emphasised the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities. Under this framework, developed nations are expected to take greater responsibility for addressing climate change and supporting developing economies. He questioned the delivery of the promised USD 100 billion annual climate financing commitment, alleging that financial support remained inadequate.
Piyush Goyal's Germany Visit
Goyal is visiting Germany and the Netherlands from October 22 to 27, accompanied by approximately 100 Indian businesses and startups. His remarks highlight continuing differences between India and Europe over carbon emissions, climate financing and trade-related environmental regulations.

Extension of Initiation of Investigations
The Petitions
On September 30, 2026, the U.S. Department of Commerce (Commerce) received antidumping duty (AD) and countervailing duty (CVD) petitions on imports of certain railway tank cars and parts thereof (tank cars) from Mexico filed in proper form on behalf of UTLX Manufacturing LLC (the petitioner), a domestic producer of tank cars.[1]
Determination of Industry Support for the Petitions
Sections 702(b)(1) and 732(b)(1) of the Tariff Act of 1930, as amended (the Act), require that a petition be filed by or on behalf of the domestic industry. To determine that the petition has been filed by or on behalf of the industry, sections 702(c)(4)(A) and 732(c)(4)(A) of the Act require that the domestic producers or workers who support the petition account for: (i) at least 25 percent of the total production of the domestic like product; and (ii) more than 50 percent of the production of the domestic like product produced by that portion of the industry expressing support for, or opposition to, the petition. Moreover, sections 702(c)(4)(D) and 732(c)(4)(D) of the Act provide that, if the petition does not establish support of domestic producers or workers accounting for more than 50 percent of the total production of the domestic like product, Commerce shall: (i) poll the industry or rely on other information in order to determine if there is support for the petition, as required by subparagraph (A); or (ii) if there is a large number of producers, determine industry support using a statistically valid sampling method to poll the industry.
Extension of Time
Sections 702(c)(1)(A) and 732(c)(1)(A) of the Act provide that within 20 days of the filing of an antidumping or countervailing duty petition, Commerce will determine,
inter alia,
whether the petition has been filed by or on behalf of the U.S. industry producing the domestic like product. Sections 702(c)(1)(B) and 732(c)(1)(B) of the Act provide that the deadline for the initiation determination, in exceptional circumstances, may be extended by 20 days in any case in which Commerce must “poll or otherwise determine support for the petition by the industry.” Because it is not clear from the Petitions whether the industry support criteria have been met, Commerce has determined it should extend the time period for determining whether to initiate the AD and CVD investigations in order to further examine the issue of industry support.
Commerce will need additional time to gather and analyze additional information regarding industry support. Therefore, it is necessary to extend the
( printed page 67289)
deadline for determining the adequacy of the Petitions by an additional 20 days. As a result, in accordance with sections 702(c)(1)(B) and 732(c)(1)(B) of the Act, Commerce's initiation determination will now be due no later than November 9, 2026.
International Trade Commission Notification
Commerce will contact the U.S. International Trade Commission (ITC) and will make this extension notice available to the ITC.

Acting Deputy Assistant Secretary for Antidumping and Countervailing Duty Operations.

AGENCY:
Enforcement and Compliance, International Trade Administration, Department of Commerce.
SUMMARY:
The U.S. Department of Commerce (Commerce) is simultaneously initiating and issuing the preliminary results of a changed circumstances review (CCR) of the antidumping duty (AD) order on heavy-walled rectangular welded carbon steel pipes and tubes (HWR) from Mexico, consistent with section 751(b) of the Tariff Act of 1930, as amended (the Act), and 19 CFR 351.216 and 351.221(c)(3)(ii). Based on the information on the record, we preliminarily determine that Perfiles LM, S.A. de C.V. (PLM) is the successor-in-interest to Perfiles y Herrajes LM, S.A. de C.V. (PyH). Interested parties are invited to comment on these preliminary results.
DATES:
Applicable October 26, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Paola Aleman Ordaz, AD/CVD Operations, Office II, Enforcement and Compliance, International Trade Administration, U.S. Department of Commerce, 1401 Constitution Avenue NW, Washington, DC 20230; telephone: 202-482-4031.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background
On September 13, 2016, Commerce published in the
Federal Register
the AD order on HWR from Mexico.[1]
On August 19, 2026, PLM informed Commerce that, effective July 11, 2017, it had changed its name from “Perfiles y Herrajes LM, S.A. de C.V.” (
i.e.,
PyH) to “Perfiles LM, S.A. de C.V.” (
i.e.,
PLM) and requested that Commerce conduct a CCR under 19 CFR 351.216(b) to determine that PLM is the successor in-interest to PyH for purposes of determining PLM's AD cash deposits and liabilities.[2]
On September 3, 2026, Commerce declined to initiate the CCR that PLM requested, citing the need for additional information pertaining to any changes in management, production facilities, customers, and suppliers.[3]
Therefore, Commerce issued a supplemental questionnaire to PLM, to which we received a timely response on September 21, 2026.[4]
We did not receive comments from other interested parties concerning this request.
Scope of the Order
The merchandise covered by the scope of the
Order
is HWR from Mexico. For a complete description of the scope of the
Order, see
the Preliminary Decision Memorandum.[5]
Initiation of Changed Circumstances Review
Pursuant to section 751(b)(1) of the Act, and 19 CFR 351.216, Commerce will conduct a CCR of an order upon receipt of information or a review request from an interested party for a review of an order which shows changed circumstances sufficient to warrant a review of the order.[6]
In the past, Commerce has used CCRs to address the applicability of cash deposit rates after there have been changes in the name or structure of a respondent, such as a merger or spinoff (“successor-in- interest,” or “successorship,” determinations).[7]
The information submitted by PLM supporting its claim that it is the successor-in-interest to PyH demonstrates changed circumstances sufficient to warrant such a review.[8]
The information submitted by PLM substantiates that its request is based solely on a change in the name of the company from “Perfiles y Herrajes LM, S.A. de C.V.” to “Perfiles LM, S.A. de C.V.” effective on July 11, 2017.[9]
Moreover, the evidence submitted in support of PLM's request demonstrates that PLM is otherwise the same business entity as PyH. Therefore, in accordance with the regulation referenced above, Commerce is initiating a CCR to determine whether PLM is the successor-in-interest to PyH.
Preliminary Results
Commerce is permitted by 19 CFR 351.221(c)(3)(ii) to combine the notice of initiation of a CCR and the preliminary results if Commerce concludes that expedited action is warranted. In this instance, because the record contains information necessary to make a preliminary finding, we find that expedited action is warranted and we have combined the notice of initiation and the preliminary results.
Accordingly, pursuant to section 751(b) of the Act, we have conducted a successor-in-interest analysis in response to PLM's request. In making a successor-in-interest determination in an AD CCR, Commerce examines several factors, including, but not limited to, changes in the following: (1) management and ownership; (2) production facilities; (3) supplier relationships; and (4) customer base.[10]
While no single factor or combination of factors will necessarily provide a dispositive indication of a successor-in-interest relationship, generally, Commerce will consider the new company to be the successor to the
( printed page 67290)
previous company if the new company's resulting operation is not materially dissimilar to that of its predecessor.[11]
Thus, if the evidence demonstrates that, with respect to the production and sales of the subject merchandise, the new company operates as essentially the same business entity as the former company, Commerce will assign to the new company the cash deposit rate of its predecessor.[12]
In its CCR request, PLM provided evidence demonstrating that PLM's operations are not materially dissimilar from those of PyH. Based on the record, we preliminarily determine that PLM is the successor-in-interest to PyH, as the change in the name was not accompanied by significant changes to its management and ownership, production, facilities, supplier relationships, or customer base. There is also no evidence of significant changes between PyH and the successor-in-interest company PLM's operations, ownership, or corporate or legal structure during the relevant period that could have impacted the successor-in-interest company's subsidy levels.[13]
Thus, we preliminarily determine that PLM operates as essentially the same business entity as PyH, that PLM is the successor-in- interest to PyH, and that PLM should receive the same AD cash deposit rate with respect to subject merchandise as its predecessor, PyH.
For a complete discussion of the information that PLM provided, and the complete successor-in-interest analysis,
see

SUMMARY:
The U.S. Department of Commerce (Commerce) is rescinding the administrative review of the countervailing duty (CVD) order on common alloy aluminum sheet (CAAS) from the People's Republic of China (China), covering the period (POR) of January 1, 2025, through December 31, 2025.
DATES:

Alexander Wolfe, AD/CVD Operations, Office VI, Enforcement and Compliance, International Trade Administration, U.S. Department of Commerce, 1401 Constitution Avenue NW, Washington, DC 20230; telephone: (202) 482-5826.
( printed page 67283)
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background
On February 6, 2019, Commerce published in the
Federal Register
the CVD order on CAAS from China.[1]
On February 2, 2026, Commerce published in the
Federal Register
a notice of opportunity to request an administrative review of the
Order
.[2]
On March 31, 2026, pursuant to requests from interested parties,[3]
Commerce initiated an administrative review with respect to four companies: Alcha International Holdings Limited (Alcha International), Jiangsu Alcha Aluminum Co., Ltd. (Jiangsu Alcha), Yantai Jintai International Trade Co., Ltd. (Yantai Jintai), and Yinbang Clad Material Co., Ltd. (Yinbang).[4]
On April 6, 2026, we placed on the record U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) data for the entries of CAAS from China during the POR and invited interested parties to comment.[5]
No interested party submitted comments regarding the CBP data. The CBP data showed that Yantai Jintai and Yinbang were the only companies subject to this administrative review with suspended entries of subject merchandise during the POR.[6]
On May 29, 2026, Yantai Jintai withdrew its request for an administrative review of itself.[7]
On June 29, 2026, the petitioner withdrew its request for an administrative review of Yinbang.[8]
No other interested party requested review of Yantai Jintai or Yinbang.
On June 30, 2026, Commerce notified interested parties that it intended to rescind the administrative review with respect to Alcha International and Jiangsu Alcha, because these companies did not have reviewable entries of subject merchandise during the POR for which liquidation is suspended.[9]
On August 3, 2026, Commerce issued a corrected notification of its intent to rescind the administrative review.[10]
No interested party submitted comments regarding Commerce's intent to rescind the administrative review.
Rescission of Review
Pursuant to 19 CFR 351.213(d)(3), it is Commerce's practice to rescind an administrative review of a CVD order where it concludes that there were no suspended entries of subject merchandise during the POR for an exporter or producer.[11]
Normally, upon completion of an administrative review, the suspended entries are liquidated at the CVD assessment rate for the review period.[12]
Therefore, for an administrative review to be conducted, there must be a reviewable, suspended entry that Commerce can instruct CBP to liquidate at the calculated CVD assessment rate for the review period.[13]
As noted above, CBP entry data showed that there were no POR entries of subject merchandise for Alcha International or Jiangsu Alcha, the only companies for which requests for review were not withdrawn. Accordingly, in the absence of reviewable, suspended entries of subject merchandise during the POR, we are rescinding this administrative review, in its entirety, in accordance with 19 CFR 351.213(d)(3).

As Commerce has proceeded to a final rescission of this administrative review, no cash deposit rates will change. Accordingly, the current cash deposit requirements shall remain in effect until further notice.
Assessment Rates
Commerce will instruct CBP to assess countervailing duties on all appropriate entries. Countervailing duties shall be assessed at rates equal to the cash deposit of estimated countervailing duties required at the time of entry, or withdrawal from warehouse, for consumption, in accordance with 19 CFR 351.212(c)(1)(i). Commerce intends to issue assessment instructions to CBP no earlier than 35 days after the date of publication of this rescission notice in the
Federal Register
.
Notification Regarding Administrative Protective Order (APO)
This notice serves as a final reminder to parties subject to an APO of their responsibility concerning the return or destruction of proprietary information disclosed under APO in accordance with 19 CFR 351.305(a)(3), which continues to govern business proprietary information in this segment of the proceeding. Timely written notification of the return or destruction of the APO materials, or conversion to judicial protective order is hereby requested. Failure to comply with regulations and terms of an APO is a violation, which is subject to sanction.
Notification to Interested Parties
This notice is issued and published in accordance with sections 751(a)(1) and 777(i)(1) of the Tariff Act of 1930, as amended, and 19 CFR 351.213(d)(4).

high_priority_articles.summary: US discreetly moves diplomats and families from multiple Middle Eastern countries as intel warns of Iranian plots  CNNIran live updates: Iranian plotting against US citizens abroad in 'advanced stages'  ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and VideosEXCLUSIVE: US orders diplomats to depart Saudi Arabia amid Houthi strikes  ReutersU.S. troops and diplomats evacuating Middle East posts, sources say  NBC NewsUS warns of Houthi threat in updated Israel travel...
high_priority_articles.full_text:
The United States is rushing to move some diplomats and their family members from posts in the Middle East as the threat of regional escalation looms, according to multiple sources familiar with the matter.
The departures have been described as a frustrating and chaotic déjà vu, as many of those leaving had only recently returned to their posts after being ordered out during the height of the Iran war.
An unclassified October 23 memo to Secretary of State Marco Rubio says US intelligence has found that “Iran has substantially increased efforts to target US personnel” and plotting efforts “have reached advanced stages in both the Middle East and certain other countries.”
A US official told CNN, “When it comes to our staffing at embassies, we constantly evaluate new information about the security environment. The threat of Houthi attacks and of Iranian terror plots targeting U.S. officials are informing our decisions on staffing adjustments for embassies on RO Status in the region.”
Axios was first to report on the unclassified memo.
“To say it has been chaotic is an understatement,” said one US diplomat, explaining that the financial support they have been offered to date does not cover the costs for moving their entire family from the region. Many of those families had scrambled then to leave their homes in the Middle East in the early weeks of the war and find new housing and schools for their kids. Now, many are having to do the same again, with what they say is potentially less financial support from the State Department.
“This echoes the chaos families experienced earlier this year. Some had barely settled back in before being told to leave again,” Nikki Gamer, the spokesperson for the American Foreign Service Association, told CNN. “They are understandably upset, confused, and angry.”
Later Friday, a State Department official confirmed that all US direct hire personnel and their families “are getting per diem allowances and support for lodging and schools, with per diem allowances consistent with government rates of where they are geographically in the country.”
The adjustments come as the Iranian-backed Houthis have increased their attacks on Saudi Arabia – hostilities which the State Department has repeatedly warned “have the potential to escalate rapidly beyond that immediate area.”
They also come as US President Donald Trump has suggested he could relaunch strikes against Iran after the midterms, and as sources said Israel has lobbied – unsuccessfully for now – for more immediate action.
The State Department this week ordered the departure of non-emergency personnel and all family members from Saudi Arabia. Officials said the ordered departure was done in response to the Houthi escalations.
At the same time, it has been quietly adjusting its staffing caps at multiple other embassies in the Middle East, including Jordan, Bahrain, Kuwait, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates, and Lebanon, sources told CNN.
A State Department official confirmed to CNN that Lebanon, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, and Jordan “will see temporary changes to staffing levels under restricted operations.” They said there are no changes to personnel in Kuwait or Bahrain, which suggest they are not over their staffing caps.
“Under Restricted Operations Status, staffing levels are constantly evaluated and adjusted,” the official said.
Unlike the Saudi Arabia ordered departure, the movements from these embassies have not been publicly announced. The State Department has stressed that those embassies, unlike Saudi Arabia, have not changed status and remain on “restricted operations” status. Even when there is no formal change in status, there can still be a change in staffing within the “restricted operations” status.
“There’s a very Groundhog Day vibe,” a source in Amman said of some embassy staff being asked to leave the Jordanian capital again.
Not all of the embassies allowed children to return to the posts, but most allowed spouses to come back. Now, the family members are leaving those embassies to which they have only recently been allowed to return – but unlike earlier this year, sources say family members are not being given the same financial support.
Communication and coordination around the departures from the department’s headquarters in Foggy Bottom to foreign service officers in the field is “just as much of a shit show” as early on in the Iran war, said one source familiar with the departures.
In the days around the adjustments, there were concerns among foreign service officers about whether the State Department will give their families “per diem” allowances for relocating to the US, the source said, noting that some embassies haven’t had the planning meetings or town halls with staff that are typical before departures.
“A lot of people are hearing about it through the news instead of their leadership at post,” the source added.
The American Foreign Service Association, the union representing foreign service officers, said it is hearing accounts “of bureaucratic ping-pong.”
“Families that had barely returned to their posts and re-enrolled their children in school are being told to prepare to evacuate again without being advised as to what level of financial support they can count on,” it said in a statement Thursday.
Gamer, the spokesperson for AFSA, told CNN that “families outside Saudi Arabia have told AFSA they are being directed to leave without confirmed housing assistance or per diem.” They have been told this is because their embassies are not changing status from “restricted operations.”
Families often rely on those allowances to help them find housing and cover the unexpected costs associated with being uprooted from their homes abroad, especially if their diplomatic family member is remaining at the embassy as an essential worker.
“Families deserve to know how they will pay for a place to live before they board a plane,” Gamer said.
The State Department official said, “We understand how hard being on Restricted Operations Status, Authorized Departure, or Ordered Departure is for our diplomatic staff and their families.”
“We are committed to using every tool available to help families navigate this difficult time, including the added expenses and school enrollment,” they said. “We are communicating directly with staff affected by these latest changes and will have more to say in the days ahead.”

TradingKey - The Federal Reserve will hold its Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting from October 27 to 28, Eastern Time. Inflationary pressures and labor market shifts have heightened monetary policy uncertainty, with the market focusing on whether the Fed will raise interest rates again and how subsequent policy signals will affect US stocks.
As of October 22, according to the CME FedWatch Tool, the market estimated an approximately 90.6% probability that the Fed would keep interest rates unchanged in October, and an approximately 9.4% probability of a 25-basis-point rate hike.
On September 16, the Fed raised the target range for the federal funds rate by 25 basis points to 3.75%–4.00%. The key focus of this meeting lies in whether the Fed will continue to tighten policy and what signals it will release regarding the future rate path.
[Source: CME]
The market currently expects the Federal Reserve to keep interest rates unchanged in October, but inflationary pressures remain an important factor influencing subsequent policy. US CPI rose 3.7% year-on-year in September, higher than August's 3.4%; core CPI rose 2.6% year-on-year, also higher than the previous reading of 2.4%, showing that inflationary pressures have not yet fully eased.
Meanwhile, slowing job growth may limit room for the Federal Reserve to tighten policy further. The Fed needs to comprehensively evaluate inflation trends, the labor market, and economic growth to balance price stability and employment goals.
According to the September dot plot, Fed officials' median forecast for the federal funds rate at the end of 2026 and 2027 was 4.1%, higher than the June forecasts of 3.8% and 3.6%. This reflects a more hawkish stance among officials regarding the future rate path compared to before, but it does not mean the Fed has committed to continuing rate hikes.
[Source: Federalreserve]
Therefore, even if rate hikes are paused in October, the risk of subsequent rate increases has not disappeared. Investors should focus on the Fed's assessment of inflation and employment, as well as whether the post-meeting statement signals further policy tightening in December.
Rising interest rates may push up Treasury yields and corporate borrowing costs, putting pressure on high-valuation growth stocks. The construction of AI data centers and GPU procurement require substantial capital investments; as a result, financing costs, project commissioning timelines, and investment returns have become key market focuses.
Take Oracle (ORCL) and CoreWeave (CRWV) as examples. In the first quarter of fiscal year 2027, Oracle's capital expenditures were approximately $28.5 billion, and free cash flow stood at negative $5.4 billion, reflecting the capital demands driven by AI infrastructure expansion. During the same period, the company's operating cash flow was approximately $23.1 billion, demonstrating that it still possesses strong operating cash flow generation capabilities.
CoreWeave, meanwhile, relies more heavily on external financing to support its data center expansion. In the second quarter of 2026, its net interest expense was approximately $640 million, making financing costs and debt service pressures key areas of concern.
If interest rates remain high for an extended period, costs for new financing and debt refinancing for certain companies may rise. However, the ultimate impact will depend on debt maturities, fixed or floating rate arrangements, and credit spreads.
For AI infrastructure companies, investors should also focus on whether revenue growth can translate into profits and cash flow, as well as whether additional capital expenditures can yield reasonable returns.
If the Federal Reserve holds interest rates steady and signals that inflation is gradually easing, growth stock valuations could find support. However, if the Fed delivers a surprise rate hike or hints at potential policy tightening in December, Treasury yields and borrowing costs may rise further, putting greater pressure on high-valuation tech stocks and AI infrastructure companies with substantial financing needs.
Investors should focus on three key metrics: first, changes in rate futures pricing for the December meeting; second, U.S. Treasury yields and corporate credit spreads to gauge shifting interest rate expectations and financing risks; and third, the capital expenditures, free cash flow, and financing arrangements of companies like Oracle and CoreWeave to assess whether AI investments can translate into actual returns.
Overall, the key to the October meeting lies not only in whether a rate hike occurs, but also in how the Federal Reserve shapes future rate expectations. For AI-related stocks, the interest rate environment must be evaluated alongside corporate earnings, cash flows, and returns on investment, making it difficult to determine future stock price trends based on a single rate decision alone.

The KOSPI index fell by 2% after experiencing sharp fluctuations last week amid controversies over the profitability of artificial intelligence (AI) investments and the re-escalation of armed conflict in the Middle East. This week, the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting and Israel's general election are scheduled, followed by the third-quarter earnings releases from SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics. Interest rates, international oil prices, and semiconductor performance are expected to determine the direction of the stock market.
According to Korea Exchange on the 25th, the KOSPI index closed at 5550.30 on the 23rd, down 117.75 points (2.08%) from Jeonju. Gains and losses alternated over the five-day period, and a buy-side sidecar (futures market circuit breaker) was triggered in the KOSPI market on the 21st. Retail investors and foreign investors made net sales of 1.1021 trillion won and 719.9 billion won, respectively, while institutional investors made net purchases of 419 billion won. Foreign investors made net sales of SK Hynix worth 863.7 billion won, while making net purchases of Samsung Electronics worth 783.8 billion won.
The burden of AI investment by major U.S. tech companies fueled stock market volatility last week. Meta's third-quarter revenue increased by 26% year-on-year, but its free cash flow (FCF—the amount of cash generated from operating activities minus capital expenditures) turned into a deficit of $2.12 billion due to large-scale capital investments. Concerns grew over whether AI capital investment could continue to expand amid high oil prices and rising market interest rates, causing the NASDAQ index to fall by 2.60% on the 22nd (local time). This was the largest drop since June this year.
On the 23rd, domestic semiconductor stocks rebounded after SK Hynix announced it would suspend its consideration of a U.S. NASDAQ listing for its grandchild company, Solidigm. As concerns over shareholder value dilution from the grandchild company's listing eased, SK Hynix closed at 1,277,000 won, up 4.42% from the previous day. Samsung Electronics also ended trading at 215,500 won, up 0.47%. On that day, the KOSPI closed with a 0.3% gain.
Events that could impact the domestic stock market are also scheduled for this week. The Federal Reserve System (Federal Reserve) will hold its FOMC meeting on the 27th and 28th (local time). President Donald Trump has intensified criticism of the Federal Reserve's monetary policy after its September rate increase, raising concerns about borrowing costs and the outlook for U.S. stocks. The dispute centers on Fed Chair Kevin Warsh and the central bank's efforts to contain inflation, with potential consequences for major indexes and investment in artificial intelligence infrastructure.
The Federal Reserve raised its benchmark interest rate by 0.25 percentage point in September, bringing the target range to 3.75%-4.00%. According to The Motley Fool, persistent inflation could prompt additional increases, while higher financing costs could slow AI data center construction, a major driver of equity market gains.
Market pricing tracked by CME Group's FedWatch Tool indicated a 64% probability of at least another 0.75 percentage point in rate increases by September 2027. The Federal Open Market Committee was scheduled to meet on October 27-28, 2026, as investors assessed the inflation outlook and the possibility of further monetary tightening.
In an interview with Time, Trump directed his criticism primarily at the Federal Reserve's board, while distinguishing Warsh from other policymakers.
"The problem is that the Fed board is very hostile" Trump said in the interview, according to the account published by Bloomberg-related news coverage.
Trump also said he did not personally blame Warsh for the board's decision and suggested the chair faced opposition within the committee.
"It's a problem because we have a very hostile Fed board," Trump said.
He added that he disagreed with the September decision and believed the board's position was contributing to tensions over monetary policy.
"I don't blame Kevin Warsh. I probably would have voted against the board if I were him," Trump said.
Trump had also expressed confidence in Warsh while arguing that the chair faced a difficult position within the committee. Speaking to reporters on September 16, the day of the rate increase, he criticized the level of borrowing costs and the board's approach.
"I'm relying on Kevin, but he's got a very tough board," Trump said.
He argued that interest rates remained too high and accused policymakers of making decisions that could harm his administration's economic performance.
"The interest rates are too high; they're not appropriate.... The board is very hostile. They're very political. They're doing the wrong thing," Trump said.
Trump also alleged that the board's decisions were politically motivated, although the source material did not establish evidence supporting that accusation.
"raising the rates to make Trump do as bad as they can possibly do," Trump said.
Inflation remains a central factor behind the Fed's decisions. According to the source reports, U.S. consumer inflation reached 4.2% in May 2026, a three-year high, and stood at 3.7% year over year in September. Both readings exceeded the Federal Reserve's long-term inflation target of 2%.
Economic pressures include tariffs introduced by the Trump administration and energy supply disruptions associated with the war involving Iran. Research from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York estimated that tariffs had added 2.9 percentage points to goods-price inflation by February 2026.
The conflict involving Iran has also disrupted energy supplies through the Strait of Hormuz, contributing to higher fuel costs. The source report said the disruption had affected a significant share of global petroleum flows and that restoring regional production and rebuilding inventories could take months.
Bond markets have reflected concerns about financing costs. The 10-year U.S. Treasury yield reached 5.34% on October 1, 2026, its highest level in 24 years, according to the source report. Long-term yields influence corporate borrowing expenses and financing for capital-intensive projects such as AI data centers.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average, S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite have recorded substantial gains during Trump's presidency.
