high_priority_articles.title: Could France's bond turmoil force the ECB's hand? - Euronews.com
high_priority_articles.summary: Could France's bond turmoil force the ECB's hand?  Euronews.com
high_priority_articles.full_text:
The European Central Bank is expected to hold rates next week as France's bond sell-off tightens borrowing conditions across the eurozone, while ECB President Christine Lagarde has made clear that the first steps to tackle French debt woes must come from Paris, not Frankfurt.
When the European Central Bank (ECB) meets next Thursday, it is widely expected to leave interest rates unchanged, partly because rising government bond yields are already pushing up borrowing costs across the eurozone.
ECB President Christine Lagarde has played down hopes of a rescue, saying the solution to France's debt problems lies at home.
The yield on France's 10-year government bond traded above 5% on Friday after rising to that level on Wednesday for the first time since 2002. The gap with German 10-year bonds, the eurozone's safest debt, was above 170 basis points.
Meanwhile, the 30-year yield was at 5.5%, and the gap with German 30-year bonds was even wider at 184 basis points.
On Thursday, the cost of France's five-year credit default swaps, contracts that insure investors against a government default, also climbed above 100 basis points for the first time since October 2012, when the eurozone was going through its sovereign debt crisis.
Lawmakers remain split over next year's budget, which includes €43 billion in spending cuts and additional revenue measures that the government has no majority to push through.
Despite the recent market movements, ratings agency Moody's maintained its Aa3 credit rating for France on Friday evening, albeit with a negative outlook. S&P and Fitch have their ratings one-notch lower.
Civil unrest is adding to investors' concerns.
More protests are expected this weekend, and Paris police prefect Patrice Faure has advised business owners in a letter to hire private security.
French trade unions, unanimously disappointed after meeting Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu on Wednesday, have called for a large mobilisation on 5 November.
Sophie Binet, head of the CGT, one of France's biggest unions, urged workers to "generalise the strike".
Bonds doing the ECB's job
The case for another rate hike is still there.
The ECB has raised rates twice this year, lifting its deposit rate to 2.5%, and eurozone inflation jumped to 3.8% in September, driven by energy prices.
Yet German yields have climbed so much since September that their effect on growth and inflation roughly matches a 25 basis point hike, Carsten Brzeski, global head of macro at Dutch bank ING, estimated in an investor note on Thursday.
"For France, it’s closer to a 50 basis point hike," Brzeski wrote, adding that "the bond market has taken over the ECB's job".
Brzeski expects the ECB to wait for new staff forecasts in December before deciding on its next hike.
ECB President Christine Lagarde told the European Parliament on 28 September that long-term rates "have risen notably, which will slow growth".
Could the ECB intervene?
ECB officials have played down the possibility of intervening to lower France's borrowing costs, but have stopped short of ruling it out.
The central bank bought government bonds during the eurozone debt crisis to stabilise markets and ensure its rate decisions continued to feed through to the economy.
Speaking on the sidelines of the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank in Bangkok last week, Lagarde said that "there are particular circumstances that lead to some countries being more affected, France being a case in point."
"The primary and first solution lies at home in France. And it has to do with fiscal policies," the ECB president added.
Banque de France governor Emmanuel Moulin went further last Friday, saying the conditions for ECB intervention were not met at that time because there was no financial fragmentation in the eurozone.
However, both officials spoke before France’s 10-year borrowing costs rose above 5%.
If the ECB decides to intervene in the French bond market, one option could be the Transmission Protection Instrument (TPI), which was created in 2022 and has never been used.
The TPI lets the ECB buy the debt of countries whose borrowing costs climb in ways it judges unjustified by their economic fundamentals and threaten the transmission of monetary policy across the eurozone.
For a country to be eligible, it needs to meet several criteria, including following EU fiscal rules and keeping its debt on a sustainable path.
France is nursing a debt-to-GDP ratio of 119.1%, and the current budget negotiations offer little prospect of a quick reduction in the deficit, which is necessary to put the debt on a sustainable path.
Meanwhile, the government expects its debt-servicing costs to rise by more than €10 billion in 2027 compared with this year.
"The bar for activating the ECB's bond-buying programme remains high," Brzeski wrote in a separate investor note last week.
He added that, for France, that would at least mean passing its full budget. Acting too early could be "interpreted as monetary financing of the debt of a country unwilling to follow the rules," he warned.
The ECB's other emergency tool, Outright Monetary Transactions (OMT), was created in 2012 at the height of the eurozone debt crisis to allow unlimited purchases of a struggling country's short-term bonds.
However, it is only available to governments that first sign up to a bailout programme from the eurozone's rescue fund, the European Stability Mechanism.
Instead, Brzeski expects the ECB to quietly pause the reduction of its bond holdings, reinvesting maturing debt flexibly as it did during the COVID-19 pandemic.
Should turmoil spread to other eurozone bond markets, Brzeski sees TPI as a last resort. If France continued to fall short of EU fiscal rules, "the ECB might even consider purchasing bonds from almost all eurozone countries, except for France," he said.
For now, Brzeski sees next week’s rate meeting as "uneventful on action but clearly not on words".

KUALA LUMPUR – With the prospect of haze enveloping some of Singaporeans’ favourite Malaysian travel destinations like Kuala Lumpur and Johor Bahru, those who want to enjoy a ringgit holiday can still visit spots with a record of cleaner air ahead of the upcoming school holidays.
While experts say it is difficult to accurately predict how the winds will blow beyond the next five days even with forecasting tools, data shows that parts of east Malaysia and some states in the north, like Perlis, Kedah and Kelantan, have been enjoying good air quality for the past fortnight.
Based on Malaysia’s Air Pollutant Index (API), where a reading below 100 is deemed safe for outdoor activities, these states have registered readings hovering around 50. In contrast, API readings in places like Kuala Lumpur average above 150.
With regular appearances on the Department of Environment’s daily rankings for locations with the lowest API readings across Malaysia, here are three places to go where the sky is blue and your dollar can be stretched.
Langkawi (Average API: 30s; Good air quality)
Called the Jewel of Kedah, Langkawi comprises a group of islands off the west coast of northern Malaysia. Its average API level in the past week is in the 30s.
“The air here is superb,” said Wendy Chin, a licensed nature guide who leads birding and kayaking tours on the island.
She recommends that visitors explore natural outdoor and recreational spots. “Tourists with a budget can go for mangrove tours, those with a limited budget can visit waterfalls and lepak,” she added, using the Malay slang for “chilling out”.

Langkawi is home to the UNESCO-listed Kilim Karst Geoforest Park and a few waterfalls, including the Seven Wells Waterfall, named after seven natural freshwater pools that resemble stone wells.
Other landmarks include the 125m-long curved suspension Sky Bridge offering views of rainforests and the Andaman Sea, as well as Cenang Beach and Dayang Bunting Island, which has a silhouette resembling a pregnant maiden.
A travel planner at My Curious Trips, who wanted to be known only as Yannick, said Langkawi offers a mix of nature, beaches, shopping and good food such as crab noodles.
Another pull factor is duty-free products like alcohol, imported chocolates and perfumes that are cheaper than on the mainland.
Balik Pulau (API: 40s; Good)
Penang is no stranger to many Singaporeans, who can likely rattle off names like Armenian Street, Batu Ferringhi and Cheong Fatt Tze Mansion like their ABCs. But it is the Balik Pulau region in the west of the island that enjoyed the cleanest air in Penang in October, with an average API reading in the mid-40s.
Balik Pulau – “the back of the island” in Malay – is located about 20km from George Town and is most conveniently accessible by car. Drivers can get there via a coastal route with beach views, or through a mountain pass with lush forests.
For those who brave the journey, Balik Pulau’s eco-tourism offers a different experience from the heritage of George Town, said Penang’s tourism and creative economy committee chairman Wong Hon Wai.
He added that Balik Pulau is especially popular during the durian season, as it is known as Penang’s durian heartland. Apart from the thorny fruit, Balik Pulau is also home to the Ghee Hup Nutmeg Factory, where visitors can sample the fruit in its jam, pickled or juice variants.
On a day with good weather, tourists can explore mangrove reserves by boat or cycle around the countryside, exploring paddy fields and fruit orchards, before ending the night with a seafood dinner.

Water activities like stand-up paddle boarding, hydrofoil surfing and parasailing against the Borneo sunset are available at the popular Tanjung Aru beach.
Unclouded skies may also open the door to early morning drives to see Malaysia’s tallest peak Mount Kinabalu from spots like the ticketed Kinabalu Park or the Pekan Nabalu lookout point. However, the end of the year may bring rain, which makes climbing the mountain less advisable.
For now, the clear air has already been restorative for some travellers.
Walking across Tanjung Aru Beach, a popular sunset spot, online advertisement executive Delphine Tan, 39, said the air in Kota Kinabalu was much better than in Kuala Lumpur. She was on a trip with her husband to visit the beaches and mountain town Kundasang, which is near Mount Kinabalu.
She told ST: “My sinusitis has not flared up here. The sunshine is nice and the air quality is good.”

high_priority_articles.title: Trump Says US Is Close to Trade Deals with Mexico and Canada as Tariff Talks Advance - Sri Lanka Guardian
high_priority_articles.summary: Trump Says US Is Close to Trade Deals with Mexico and Canada as Tariff Talks Advance  Sri Lanka Guardian
high_priority_articles.full_text:
US President Donald Trump said on Friday that Washington was close to reaching a trade agreement with Mexico and that negotiations with Canada were also progressing, as the three North American countries seek to resolve tensions over tariffs and trade rules.
“We are close to reaching an agreement with Mexico. It will be a very good agreement, hopefully for them too, but it will certainly be a good agreement for us,” Trump said at the White House before travelling to Fort Myer, Florida, for an election rally. He said Canada was also working hard to secure a deal with the United States.
“Although I hate to say it, we have all the cards in our favour in both cases,” he added.
The negotiations centre on a framework to reduce tariffs affecting the automotive and steel industries, both important to the economies of Mexico and Canada. The talks have gained urgency since Washington announced in July that it would not renew the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA), which Trump signed during his first presidency in 2020.
Negotiations between Washington and Mexico City accelerated after media reports last week suggested that discussions had stalled because of opposition from US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. According to The Wall Street Journal, the two countries had been close to an agreement under which the United States would reduce tariffs on steel, aluminium and automobiles in exchange for concessions from Mexico. Disagreements over duties on vehicles and metals reportedly prevented the deal from advancing.
Trump has sought to portray the remaining differences as manageable. Speaking at an election rally in Kansas on Monday, he said the United States would not lose $150 billion through its trade deficit with Mexico. Referring to the deficit, he declared that Washington was close to a major agreement that could reduce the figure dramatically, “maybe to zero”.
Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum said on Tuesday that the countries were also “very close” to an agreement, while stressing that several issues remained unresolved. She said Washington wanted to rebalance trade, whereas Mexico was seeking the greatest possible reduction in existing tariffs on vehicles, steel and aluminium, as well as assurances that no additional duties would be imposed.
“There are still issues that we have not fully resolved because we want what is best for Mexico,” Sheinbaum said. She added that the US administration had shown a constructive attitude towards the negotiations.
The three countries have spent months discussing arrangements to replace the USMCA, which Trump described during his first term as the best trade agreement in history. Since returning to the White House for a second term, however, he has pursued changes to trade rules intended to benefit US industries. The countries have consequently shifted towards bilateral negotiations.
Mexican officials remain optimistic that an agreement can be reached before the end of the year. Economy Secretary Marcelo Ebrard said last week that he hoped to secure more flexible US tariffs on Mexican vehicle and steel exports.
The automotive sector is particularly concerned about the 25% US tariff on vehicles that fail to meet the USMCA’s rules of origin. Under the existing agreement, 75% of a vehicle’s components must originate in North America for it to qualify for tariff-free treatment. Washington wants to raise that threshold to about 82%, while also demanding that half of the components come from US factories. The proposals are intended to exclude Chinese and European components but would impose additional requirements on manufacturers operating across the region.
Mexico also faces a 50% US tariff on steel under Section 232 of US trade law, alongside a general 10% tariff imposed on the country under Section 301.
Sheinbaum’s government has pursued high-level diplomatic discussions to secure tariff reductions without derailing negotiations. As a gesture of goodwill, Mexico has temporarily suspended its 10% tariff on imported automotive components, even as it continues pressing Washington to ease restrictions on its exports.

high_priority_articles.summary: South Korean, Japanese Business Leaders Adopt Joint Statement Tying CPTPP, LNG, AI Into 'New 60 Years'…Joint Response to US-China Risks  BigGo Finance
high_priority_articles.full_text:
South Korea's and Japan's leading business organizations held the 33rd Korea-Japan Business Conference at the FKI Tower in Yeouido, Seoul, on the 23rd and adopted a joint statement aimed at jointly responding to trade uncertainty and instability in energy supply chains. At the meeting, the two countries' business communities took up as key agenda items emergency liquefied natural gas (LNG) cargo swaps, the identification of joint projects in artificial intelligence (AI) and semiconductors, and cooperation on South Korea's bid to join the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP).
The theme of this year's conference was "The Prologue to a New 60 Years: A New Horizon for Korea-Japan Economic Cooperation." The vision is to build a framework for cooperation over the next 60 years, going beyond the 60 years since the normalization of diplomatic relations in 1965. Attending from South Korea were Ryu Jin, chairman of the Federation of Korean Industries, and South Korean Trade, Industry and Energy Minister Kim Jung-kwan; from Japan, Yoshinobu Tsutsui, chairman of Keidanren (Japan Business Federation), was present. The heads of major companies from both countries also attended, including Shinhan Financial Group Chairman Jin Ok-dong, Samyang Group Chairman Kim Yoon, Hyosung Group Chairman Cho Hyun-joon, Youngone Vice Chairwoman Sung Rae-eun, Sumitomo Chemical Chairman Keiichi Iwata, Sony Group Chairman Kenichiro Yoshida and Hitachi Chairman Toshiaki Higashihara.
In his opening remarks, Chairman Ryu said, "If the past 60 years were mainly a time of shuttling across the Korea Strait, I hope the next 60 years will be a time of new cooperation in which we look together beyond the horizon." He presented three major cooperation tasks: cooperation on international norms and economic security, strengthening supply-chain and energy security, and responding to common social problems. The idea is to jointly respond to US trade policy and digital regulations while checking supply risks for key items and establishing a system of mutual support in emergencies.
The Japanese side also stressed the importance of maintaining the free-trade order. Chairman Tsutsui said, "As South Korea and Japan are both highly dependent on external markets, we must cooperate to expand a free and open trade and investment environment." He emphasized the need to reform the World Trade Organization (WTO) and to deepen and expand multilateral economic partnership agreements, while expressing strong expectations for South Korea's application to join the CPTPP.
The South Korean government also called for strategic solidarity. In his keynote speech, Minister Kim said, "Deepening US-China strategic competition and geopolitical instability are expanding instability in global supply chains," and stressed that the two countries should cooperate on resource procurement and supply-chain stabilization and speak with one voice on changes in the trade order. He also proposed cooperation that leverages the two countries' strengths in the field of physical AI.
In the trade area, the two sides agreed to broaden the scope of their joint response. The Federation of Korean Industries joined a joint statement led by Keidanren supporting the extension of the US-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA). There was also a view that the "Korea-US-Japan Business Dialogue," which conveys a joint position to the US government and Congress, should be restarted as soon as possible. Also on the discussion table were the need to establish international rules on cross-border data flows and AI, and the need for a joint response to US and European Union (EU) supply-chain and advanced-industry regulations.
Energy cooperation will proceed along two tracks: crisis response and the identification of joint projects. The two sides discussed ways to strengthen emergency LNG cargo swaps based on cooperation between South Korea's Korea Gas Corporation and Japanese energy company JERA, and to expand such swaps to third-country transactions. Proposals were also made to establish hydrogen certification, standards and safety criteria, and to cooperate on stockpiling critical minerals and crisis response. There was also an idea to combine South Korean, US and Japanese technology and capital to identify joint projects in energy, semiconductors and AI data centers.
Common challenges such as low birth rates, an aging population and shrinking regional populations were also major agenda items. The meeting discussed ways to use corporate data to connect financial support to regional companies with high growth potential and to expand sales channels through the two countries' financial and distribution networks. For the "Korea-Japan Startup Cooperation Forum," which is being pushed to resume next year, the two sides decided to invite regional companies from both countries to increase transactions with companies and investors in the other country.
The significance of this agreement is that the two countries' business communities have elevated external shocks — US-China strategic competition and the fragmentation of supply chains — to a joint-response agenda rather than leaving them to individual countries. In particular, emergency LNG cargo swaps are seen as a card that can have a practical effect in easing short-term supply shocks, given that both countries are among the world's largest LNG importers. However, the joint statement is a non-binding, declarative document, so follow-up negotiations between companies will be needed before it leads to actual cargo-swap contracts or an expansion into third-country transactions.
South Korea's CPTPP accession is an issue that requires unanimous consent from all member countries despite Japan's expression of support, so immediate progress is difficult to expect. The practical achievement of this meeting is seen as the business communities' ability to help open the way for government-to-government negotiations. The joint AI data center and semiconductor projects also have not disclosed specific investment sizes or participating companies, so follow-up discussions will need to be watched.
The two countries' business communities are expected to review the implementation of the agenda items discussed this time at next year's conference. The Korea-Japan Business Conference began in 1962 and has established itself as a regular channel for private-sector economic cooperation between the two countries. This joint statement differs from previous meetings in that it bundles trade, energy, advanced industries and regional revitalization into a single cooperation package.
